faq.q: Is this tool a substitute for a risk assessment?
faq.a: No — it walks the standard decision logic (environment, traffic speed, light) to give you a well-reasoned starting point. Your employer's risk assessment and the site's rules are the documents that decide, and they override the tool wherever they're stricter.

faq.q: Why does night work push the answer to Class 3?
faq.a: Poor light degrades the daytime (fluorescent) half of hi-vis performance, so the standard's logic leans on greater visible area and more retroreflective tape — which is what Class 3 provides. Night work around any vehicle movement is Class 3 territory.

faq.q: The tool says Class 2 but my site demands Class 3 — who's right?
faq.a: The site. Principal contractors and operators are free to set stricter requirements than the risk-based minimum, and many standardise on Class 3 for simplicity or winter practicality. The stricter rule always wins.

faq.q: Why does the tool never suggest SB?
faq.a: SB is the bare toe-cap minimum with none of the antistatic, heel-cushioning or closed-seat features that S1 adds — and the price difference is trivial. In practice there's no working environment where SB is the right specification over S1.

faq.q: What if my site just says 'S3 boots required'?
faq.a: Then S3 it is — site rules override risk-based logic, and many principal contractors mandate S3 with ankle support as a blanket policy. The tool is most useful where nobody has specified anything and someone has to decide.

faq.q: Are safety trainers a code of their own?
faq.a: No — a safety trainer is a style, not a rating. An S1P trainer carries exactly the same certified toe cap and midsole as an S1P boot. What you give up is ankle coverage and weather resistance, which is why trainers suit the dry-indoor answers.

faq.q: Is this checklist a risk assessment?
faq.a: No — it's the kit consequence of hazards you already know about, with the right standard named per item. The risk assessment itself identifies and prioritises hazards, considers controls before PPE, and governs what's actually required.

faq.q: Why does every item name a standard?
faq.a: Because 'gloves' isn't a specification — EN 388 cut level C is. Naming the standard turns a checklist into an orderable list and stops the classic failure of buying kit that pattern-matches the hazard without actually being rated for it.

faq.q: What if my job's hazard isn't listed?
faq.a: The tool covers the nine most common workwear-relevant hazards. Specialist risks — arc flash, chainsaw work, molten metal, work at height — have their own guides on this site and their own certified kit; start from the standards hub or ask us.

pages.lede: Every garment ships with its washing instructions written in five little pictograms — and workwear punishes you for guessing, because the wrong wash strips flame resistance, fades hi-vis below its class and delaminates waterproofs while everything still looks fine. Pick the symbol below and get the translation.

It governs

blocks.html: The pictogram system used on UK garment labels follows the international care-labelling convention (ISO 3758). Symbols shown on a garment's own label always take precedence over any general guide, this tool included.

faq.q: What does the number in the wash tub mean?
faq.a: The maximum wash temperature in degrees Celsius — it's a ceiling, not a target. A bar under the tub means use a gentler, reduced-agitation cycle at that temperature; two bars, gentler still.

faq.q: What does the triangle with two lines mean?
faq.a: Oxygen or non-chlorine bleach only. Oxygen-based whiteners are fine; chlorine bleach is prohibited — on poly-cotton it causes yellowing and fibre damage rather than whitening.

faq.q: Why do hi-vis labels say do not tumble dry?
faq.a: Tumble heat accelerates fading of the fluorescent dye and degrades the retroreflective tape — both of which the garment's EN ISO 20471 class depends on. Line drying preserves the certification; the dryer quietly erodes it.

faq.q: What happens if you ignore a care label on PPE?
faq.a: The garment can drop below the performance its standard promises while looking perfectly fine — faded hi-vis that no longer meets its class, FR treatment stripped by the wrong detergent, waterproof membranes cooked by tumble heat. With protective kit, the care label is part of the safety spec.

faq.q: How many uniforms should an employee have?
faq.a: Enough clean sets to bridge the gap between washes, plus one spare. Five shifts with a weekly wash means five or six sets; washing every couple of days brings it down to about four. Hygiene-critical kit — chef whites, scrubs — adds one more, because it can't be re-worn between washes.

faq.q: How much spare uniform should a business hold?
faq.a: Around 5% of the total order (minimum a couple of sets), spread across the sizes you actually employ. Spares absorb stains, snags and new starters without triggering an emergency reorder — which matters double for embroidered kit, where replacements aren't next-day.

faq.q: Does buying more sets per person save money?
faq.a: Over the garment's life, usually yes. Each extra set in the rotation cuts the number of washes every garment takes, and washing is what ages workwear — colour, print, tape and treatment all fade per cycle. Bigger order, slower replacement clock.
